source_user: Explain how prefill interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Two trade-offs are: (1) capacity pressure—KV entries grow with layers, cached tokens, KV heads, head dimension, and element size, so long contexts or many concurrent sequences can exhaust device memory and trigger eviction/paging or lower batch size; (2) bandwidth and lifecycle overhead—the decoder must read the retained tensors and allocate, copy, or shard them, so at high concurrency the workload may become memory-bandwidth or communication limited rather than compute limited. Mechanism: each decode step appends the new token's per-layer K/V and the query attends over the accumulated cache. Boundary condition: reuse is correct only for the same compatible model, attention/position configuration, and exact prefix; a changed prefix or incompatible positional state requires invalidation. Check these claims with cache-size accounting and matched cache-on/off tests varying context length and concurrency; record peak memory, paging/evictions, prefill and inter-token latency, throughput, and tail percentiles. Treat any speedup or memory estimate as workload- and implementation-dependent until measured.
risks: Memory and bandwidth behavior varies with precision, paging, sharding, and kernel implementation.
A cache-on/off comparison can be misleading if scheduling or output tokens are not matched.
evidence_required: Cache accounting plus peak-memory and eviction telemetry.
Controlled workload sweep over context length, batch/concurrency, and cache policy.
